title: The local three-dimensional stress in a flowing material, without assuming the constitutive law

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a way to recover the local three-dimensional stress throughout a flowing material, including how that stress changes with time, without inserting the constitutive equation being tested. A constitutive equation specifies how a material's deformation and history produce stress. Measuring stress independently would allow that equation to be tested against experimental stress fields rather than used to generate the fields against which it is assessed. The target is all six independent components of the symmetric Cauchy-stress tensor: three normal components and three shear components.

This is an inverse measurement problem. Flow birefringence—the change in optical response caused by oriented microstructure—provides two path-integrated optical observables. These do not uniquely determine six local stress components without additional information. Classical integrated photoelasticity has therefore relied on assumptions such as axisymmetric or two-dimensional flow, constitutive relations, or restrictive regularization. Multi-angle measurements and physical constraints offer a route toward recovering more of the internal stress field, but reconstruction still depends on the information content and validity of those constraints.

Independence from the constitutive equation does not mean independence from all assumptions or calibration. A method must disclose its optical or tracer response, pressure reference, boundary information, and reconstruction priors. In particular, a relation between birefringence and instantaneous stress cannot simply be presumed valid when microstructure retains or relaxes its orientation during unsteady flow. The complete innovation would combine sufficient measurement information with a validated interpretation of that information over a clearly stated material and flow domain.

significance.text: The central advance would be to make spatial stress fields experimentally accessible with independently established accuracy. Velocity-based stress inference requires a constitutive relation, while birefringence-based inference requires a validated optical response and adequate optical access. An independent volumetric stress measurement would let researchers compare theories directly with the quantity those theories predict, exposing errors that could remain hidden in velocity fields or integrated forces.

Where stress is accurately resolved at an interface, it also determines the traction acting on that interface. This would connect internal flow structure to forces on vessel walls, cell layers, submerged objects, or processing boundaries such as a die lip. The consequence is conditional on resolving interface stress accurately: a successful reconstruction in the interior does not automatically establish reliable wall or surface forces, especially where boundary discrepancies remain.

Conditional synthesis: broader access to local stress could improve the diagnosis of processing failures, interpretation of biological flows, and development of constitutive theories. Those possibilities require additional advances in material compatibility, optical or alternative measurement access, resolution, and validation. Recovering a stress field alone would neither identify a unique constitutive law nor establish clinical or industrial readiness. The revolutionary aspect is the proposed measurement capability; broad deployment remains a further research and engineering objective.

missing_breakthrough.text: The unsolved capability is independently validated recovery of all six local stress components in general non-axisymmetric, time-dependent flow without imposing the constitutive equation under investigation. The immediate scientific barrier is identifiability: determining which stress fields the observations and physical constraints can distinguish, and which apparent solutions depend on regularization or prior assumptions. Momentum balance, continuity, pressure information, and boundary data can constrain the problem, but their use must be distinguished from independent evidence that the reconstructed local field is correct.

Extending the demonstrated optical approach to unsteady materials requires more than adding time as an input. The U-FlowPET manuscript identifies the need to include temporal dimensions and particle-orientation history in the optical response. The separate oscillatory-flow experiments show why: microstructural relaxation and loading history can change birefringence, and correspondence with accumulated deformation emerged only at sufficiently large Deborah number in the tested conditions. A general method must establish how its signal relates to stress in the particular material and regime being measured, rather than assume an instantaneous universal inversion.

Material assumptions embedded in calibration and regularization are another barrier. U-FlowPET uses a stress-optic forward map, pressure-drop and flow-rate constraints, and a weak prior encouraging the deviatoric stress and strain-rate tensors to share principal directions. Its optical coefficients were calibrated against an analytical power-law pipe-flow stress field. Removing an explicit constitutive equation from the reconstruction loss is therefore a meaningful step, but it does not yet establish that the method can recover arbitrary stress orientations or unknown material behavior without model-dependent calibration.

Transmission photoelasticity also requires sufficient optical access. This restricts measurement depth and usable sample geometry, but does not categorically exclude blood, melts, or slurries from every optical method. The supplied review reports that the Nature article's author response explicitly discusses blood as a potentially birefringent complex fluid and explains that sufficiently thin samples can transmit light even when the bulk medium is not highly transparent. That qualification does not demonstrate unrestricted volumetric stress recovery in opaque bulk material. Acoustic, magnetic, or tracer-based counterparts remain proposed routes whose signals would need their own validated connection to stress.

current_state.text: On 22 May 2026, Kumagai, Tagawa, and coauthors introduced U-FlowPET in the preprint Full-component reconstruction of three-dimensional fluid stress tensors. The supplied record identifies no journal DOI for this work. The method reports reconstruction of six stress components from multi-angle photoelasticity while enforcing momentum balance and continuity, without labeled stress training data or an explicit constitutive equation in the reconstruction loss. This is a substantial demonstrated component of the proposed capability within its benchmark domain.

The preprint reports normalized mean absolute errors below 4% for an analytical pipe-flow benchmark, 10–18% for simulated curved-pipe flow, and below 8% for experimental pipe-flow measurements. The normalization uses a characteristic ground-truth deviatoric-tensor norm; these numbers are not componentwise relative percentage errors. They describe performance against the study's benchmark references and should not be interpreted as independent validation of local stress in an unknown material.

The demonstrated formulation assumes steady, incompressible viscous flow without elastic effects. Its stress-optic mapping, pressure-drop and flow-rate constraints, stress–strain-rate alignment prior, and calibration against analytical power-law pipe-flow stresses all matter to the interpretation of constitutive independence. Boundary discrepancies remain. The study therefore establishes a steady-flow reconstruction result, while leaving general unsteady behavior, elastic effects, broader stress orientations, and opaque-fluid reconstruction beyond its demonstrated scope.

On 24 October 2025, Noto, Ohie, and Tasaka published Unsteady flows uncover the limits of the stress-optic law in Nature Communications 16, 9418. Their oscillatory xanthan-gum experiments showed microstructural history and relaxation effects in birefringence, with reliable correspondence to accumulated deformation only at sufficiently large Deborah number in the tested conditions. Deborah number compares a material's relaxation time with the relevant flow timescale. The experiments primarily compared birefringence with shear rate and accumulated strain; they did not directly validate every component of the stress tensor. The lowest reported Deborah number was 1.5, so the study does not establish a universal failure threshold at or below unity.

The evidence described here comes from the supplied review of retained manuscript and article text, including supporting material and the relevant author response. The source index reports complete text extraction without recorded extraction issues, but the review did not visually inspect figures or movies; the numerical error ranges above were supported by explicit prose. No bounded freshness search was supplied, so these dated studies cannot establish the complete state of the field as of 1 November 2026 or rule out subsequent advances.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: reconstruct all six Cauchy-stress components on a three-dimensional grid in a non-axisymmetric, time-dependent flow without inserting the constitutive equation being tested. Report spatial and temporal resolution, uncertainty, the pressure reference, measurement geometry, optical or tracer calibration, boundary inputs, and every reconstruction prior. Explain which components and spatial scales the observations actually constrain. These are proposed evaluation requirements, not established community standards.
completion_criteria.label: Recover six-component volumetric unsteady stress without the tested constitutive equation

completion_criteria.text: Proposed independent validation: withhold at least one force measurement from reconstruction, then compare it with the force obtained by integrating reconstructed surface traction—for example, the measured drag on a submerged object. Add checks sensitive to local errors, since spatially compensating errors can produce the correct net force. A convincing result would demonstrate agreement within stated uncertainties across multiple conditions, with a clear account of which validation measurements were withheld from fitting and calibration.
completion_criteria.label: Validate reconstructed stress using withheld forces and local-error-sensitive checks

completion_criteria.text: Proposed unsteady test: include a material and forcing condition at Deborah number of order one or smaller, and establish the optical response's validity or failure for that particular system. The numerical target is a proposed challenge condition, not a universal stress-optic failure boundary. A fluid measured without an added birefringent tracer would be a useful additional demonstration, but tracer absence alone would not establish recovery of unsteady stress or resolve microstructural memory.
completion_criteria.label: Test optical-response validity at Deborah number order one or smaller

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and scope test: make the calibration, reconstruction procedure, raw measurement data, and uncertainty analysis sufficiently available for independent replication. Challenge the method across geometries, material responses, and stress orientations that test its stated priors. Report practical limits in optical depth, resolution, noise, boundary accuracy, and temporal response. Finite experiments would establish demonstrated breadth within those limits, rather than literal universality across flowing materials.
completion_criteria.label: Enable independent replication and report demonstrated scope and practical limits

completion_criteria.text: Proposed opaque-fluid counterpart: an acoustic, magnetic, or tracer-based method would need to recover the same local stress information and pass independent force and local-accuracy checks. Demonstrating a non-optical signal or an integrated force estimate would not alone meet the volumetric objective. Any successful result should state the material class, penetration depth, calibration dependence, and flow regime over which stress recovery has been established.
completion_criteria.label: Recover volumetric stress in opaque fluids with independently validated accuracy

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: RHE-01, A constitutive closure that still works in a flow it was not fitted to, concerns predictive material laws. RHE-07 concerns independent access to the stress fields needed to test such laws. Stress measurements could constrain or reject candidate closures, but do not by themselves identify a unique law. Only RHE-01's title was supplied, so the detailed overlap remains provisional.

Roster-based synthesis: RHE-02 on amorphous yielding, RHE-03 on dense particulate flow, RHE-10 on magma containing crystals and bubbles, and RHE-11 on ring-polymer topology each concern a particular material theory or flow regime. Accurate local stress could provide evidence for those theories where a suitable measurement modality exists. Their predictive objectives remain distinct from RHE-07's measurement objective, and the supplied optical results do not establish applicability to all those materials.

Roster-based synthesis: RHE-04 on inverse molecular design of nonlinear polymer-melt rheology and RHE-05 on active-stress theory invertible for a mechanical task concern designing molecular structure or active mechanical behavior. RHE-07 could supply experimental stress fields to evaluate those designs, but would not itself solve either inverse-design problem. Active materials and polymer melts would require validation of the measurement response in their own regimes.

Roster-based synthesis: RHE-06 concerns addressable solid–fluid switching that persists without a sustaining field or settling particles. Spatial stress measurements could help characterize switching and the resulting mechanical state. Creating and maintaining that state remains a separate material capability from observing its stress.

Roster-based synthesis: RHE-08 on elasto-inertial turbulence and drag-reduction limits and RHE-09 on computing viscoelastic flow at processing-relevant elasticity concern prediction and computation. RHE-07 could provide experimental validation fields for both. Its demonstrated steady, nonelastic formulation does not establish the temporal resolution or elastic-flow capability those applications would require.

Provisional comparison from the supplied research: historical item 4, described as an artifact-free rheometry protocol, would improve confidence in boundary measurements. Such measurements can constrain or independently validate a volumetric reconstruction, but reliable boundary rheometry does not itself reveal the internal stress field. The historical item's text was not supplied, so its exact identity, scope, and overlap cannot be verified.

change_log.change: Preserved the RHE-07 identity and framed the complete innovation as a proposed measurement capability with a demonstrated steady-flow component.
change_log.reason: The supplied evidence supports meaningful progress without establishing general time-dependent, constitutively independent volumetric stress measurement.

change_log.change: Qualified constitutive independence by adding the optical forward map, pressure and flow constraints, coaxiality prior, and analytical power-law calibration.
change_log.reason: Absence of an explicit constitutive equation in the reconstruction loss does not imply freedom from material assumptions or model-dependent calibration.

change_log.change: Retained all three reported error ranges and clarified their normalization and benchmark scope.
change_log.reason: The review supports the numbers but identifies a characteristic deviatoric-tensor normalization rather than componentwise relative errors or independent unknown-material validation.

change_log.change: Restricted the unsteady optical conclusions to the tested oscillatory xanthan-gum conditions and stated the lowest reported Deborah number of 1.5.
change_log.reason: The evidence does not establish universal stress-optic failure at modest Deborah number or a threshold at or below unity.

change_log.change: Replaced categorical exclusion of blood, melts, and slurries with an optical-access limitation.
change_log.reason: The reviewed author response allows sufficiently thin transmitting samples and discusses blood as potentially birefringent, without demonstrating unrestricted opaque-bulk reconstruction.

change_log.change: Strengthened the proposed completion demonstration with withheld validation, local-error checks, uncertainty, pressure reference, calibration disclosure, and reproducibility.
change_log.reason: A net-force match can conceal local errors, and neither absence of added tracer nor a finite test suite establishes general unsteady capability or universality.

change_log.change: Separated direct scientific consequences from conditional physiological, industrial, and alternative-modality possibilities.
change_log.reason: Broader deployment requires additional access, material-response, resolution, and validation advances.

change_log.reason: The supplied roster supports conceptual distinctions, but not detailed verification of other innovations' scope.

change_log.reason: These limitations affect publication status, completeness of the current-state assessment, and the basis for interpreting reported results.

unresolved_issues: Whether developments after the supplied studies have demonstrated broader unsteady, elastic, or opaque-fluid stress recovery is unknown; no freshness search was supplied.
The extent to which local stress remains identifiable when the coaxiality prior or analytical power-law calibration is unsuitable has not been established by the supplied benchmarks.
Independent local validation in an unknown material, including reliable boundary stresses and pressure referencing, remains to be demonstrated within the proposed broader scope.
The material-specific relation between optical response, stress, deformation history, and relaxation requires further validation; no universal Deborah-number boundary is established.
The feasibility and practical limits of acoustic, magnetic, or tracer-based full-stress reconstruction in opaque bulk fluids remain open.
Detailed overlap with the other roster entries cannot be verified from titles alone, and the text identifying historical item 4 was not supplied.

brief.title: Mapping internal forces throughout a flowing material
possible: Researchers could map stress—the pushes and sliding forces per unit area—throughout a flowing material as it changes over time. They could measure it without first assuming the rule linking the material’s deformation to its stress.
why: Researchers could test theories against the internal forces they predict. This could expose mistakes hidden by measurements of motion or total force, helping explain processing failures and biological flows.
Accurate stress maps at surfaces would connect what happens inside a flow to forces on vessel walls, cell layers and submerged objects.

sources.who: Shunsuke Kumagai, Yoshiyuki Tagawa and colleagues
sources.showed: Their preprint reconstructs all six stress components from light measurements taken at different angles, constrained by fluid mechanics. It tests steady pipe flows without putting an explicit material deformation-to-stress equation into the reconstruction.

sources.cited_for: A demonstrated route to reconstructing internal stress from light measurements and physical constraints.
sources.not_established: It does not establish independently accurate local stress in unknown materials, changing flows or flows with elastic effects.

sources.who: Daisuke Noto, Kohei Ohie and Yuji Tasaka
sources.showed: Experiments with oscillating xanthan-gum solutions showed that the light response depends on microscopic structures relaxing and retaining deformation history. A simple link between light and stress can fail in changing flows.
sources.quote: Here, we question such a paradigm by demonstrating the failure of the law in unsteady flows through laboratory experiments.
sources.cited_for: The light response needs validation when a flow changes with time.
sources.not_established: The experiments did not directly validate every stress component or establish a universal threshold for failure.

shown: Kumagai, Tagawa and colleagues’ U-FlowPET preprint reconstructs all six stress components in steady pipe-flow benchmarks, including a curved pipe and experimental measurements. Its calibration and assumptions about stress direction still constrain what the result establishes.
missing: Independent validation of local stress throughout an asymmetric, changing flow without assuming the material rule being tested is still missing.
A validated link between light signals and stress is needed when microscopic structures retain deformation history.
Accurate surface stresses and pressure references still need independent checks across broader materials and flow conditions.
Full internal stress maps with independently validated accuracy remain to be demonstrated in opaque bulk fluids.

milestones.label: Complete internal stress maps in changing, asymmetric flows
milestones.explanation: A demonstration would have to recover all six stress components throughout a changing, asymmetric flow, with resolution, uncertainty and assumptions stated. This would establish the target measurement without assuming the material rule.

milestones.label: Agreement with independent forces and local accuracy checks
milestones.explanation: Reconstructed stresses would have to match force measurements withheld from fitting and pass checks sensitive to local errors across conditions. This would prevent compensating mistakes from hiding behind a correct total force.

milestones.label: A tested light response when material relaxation matters
milestones.explanation: Tests would have to establish whether the light response remains valid when material relaxation time divided by flow timescale is near one or below. This would test the measurement where microscopic memory matters.

milestones.label: Independent replication across materials, shapes and stress directions
milestones.explanation: Independent teams would have to reproduce results using shared data and procedures across geometries, materials and stress directions, with practical limits reported. This would establish the method’s demonstrated breadth.

milestones.label: Accurate internal stress maps in opaque fluids
milestones.explanation: A method using sound, magnetic signals or added markers would have to recover local stress throughout opaque fluids and pass independent force and local accuracy checks. This would extend the capability beyond light-transmitting samples.

uncertain: Can the measurements distinguish the true local stress when calibration or assumed alignment between stress and deformation is unsuitable?
How does the link between light response and stress vary with material, deformation history and relaxation?
What depth, resolution and accuracy could sound, magnetic signals or added markers achieve in opaque fluids?

page.title: Time-resolved three-dimensional fluid stress tensor measurement
page.definition: A method recovers all six independent components of the symmetric Cauchy stress tensor—the local force per unit area on any plane—through a fluid volume as it changes in time. It does so without using the constitutive equation under test, which relates deformation history to stress.

goal.need: A single flow-birefringence projection provides fewer independent observables than the stress field contains. Inferring stress from velocity instead requires a constitutive equation. Measuring stress independently would provide experimental data against which to test that equation.

figures.caption: Information measured and information sought in optical stress reconstruction.
figures.note: These counts do not establish how many viewing angles make the reconstruction unique.

completion.title: Independent local measurements validate all six stresses in a non-axisymmetric, time-dependent flow.
completion.criterion: In one experimental non-axisymmetric, time-dependent flow, recover all six local Cauchy-stress components throughout a specified volume and time interval without using the constitutive equation under test. Independent local reference measurements, withheld from calibration and reconstruction, must agree component by component within combined stated measurement uncertainties at the claimed spatial and temporal resolution. A measured pressure reference fixes the hydrostatic offset. Agreement with integrated force alone does not meet this test.
completion.set_by: Atlas; no externally published acceptance test was located for the combined capability.
completion.basis: Searches of ISO and ASTM listings, rheology roadmaps and society material, JST PRESTO goals, and developer papers found no acceptance test for this capability. This Atlas test limits the claim to one specified material and flow. It extends the developers' three-dimensional measurement goal to the unsteady regime their formulation leaves open; it sets no universal percentage-error cutoff.

milestones.title: Laboratory measurements establish a fluid's optical response to shear along the light path.
milestones.criterion: Establish a quantitative optical response to imposed fluid shear along the light path in a controlled laboratory geometry. The paper published on 20 September 2024 tested two aqueous cellulose-nanocrystal concentrations, 0.5 and 1.0 wt%, using 1000-frame averages, and fitted the measured response to flow strength. A preprint submitted on 19 September 2026 attributes concentration-dependent stress–optical relations in these suspensions to stress partitioning; it is not peer reviewed. These results concern the measurement response, rather than recovery of all six stresses.
milestones.set_by: Atlas; searches of rheo-optical experiments and standards found no qualification threshold for this laboratory stage.

milestones.title: All six local stress components are reconstructed from laboratory measurements in steady flow.
milestones.criterion: Recover six local stresses from laboratory data without an explicit constitutive equation in the reconstruction loss. The preprint of 22 May 2026 reports three steady-flow benchmarks: analytical pipe flow, simulated curved-pipe flow, and experimental pipe flow, with normalized mean absolute errors below 4%, 10–18%, and below 8%, respectively. Errors use the spatially averaged Frobenius norm of reference deviatoric stress, not componentwise relative error. Experimental acquisition used 12 angles. Power-law calibration and a stress–strain-rate alignment prior constrain the result. The errors are results, not acceptance limits; the preprint is not peer reviewed.
milestones.set_by: Atlas; searches of developer benchmarks, standards and programme documents found no externally defined pass criterion for six-component laboratory reconstruction.

milestones.title: All six local stresses are reconstructed in an experimental non-axisymmetric, time-dependent flow.
milestones.criterion: Recover all six local stress components from experimental data in a non-axisymmetric, time-dependent flow without inserting the constitutive equation under test; retain a calibrated response that accounts for deformation history. Independent local validation remains the completion step. The paper published on 24 October 2025 tested three xanthan-gum concentrations, 0.1, 0.2 and 0.4 wt%, at 0.25, 0.5 and 1 Hz; it found a history-dependent optical response rather than full stress recovery.
milestones.set_by: Atlas; searches of unsteady rheo-optical experiments and developer extensions found no published six-component qualification protocol or universal Deborah-number threshold.

not_found: No independent local validation of all six Cauchy-stress components in a non-axisymmetric, time-dependent fluid flow was located.
The publisher's full text and PMC copy of Noto and colleagues' paper were inaccessible; its PubMed abstract and figure captions were accessible.
